text: GlideRecord is easy to write correctly and easy to write slowly. This lesson covers four well-documented performance pitfalls, and the fix for each one.

This is the single most damaging GlideRecord mistake, and it's easy to write by accident. Querying core_company once, then querying incident again inside the loop, once per company — with 500 companies, that's 501 total queries, one to get the companies plus one more per company. This is called an N plus 1 pattern, and it scales terribly: doubling the number of companies doubles the number of queries, not just the work.

The fix is one query total. Query incident once, with no per-company condition at all, then group the counts in memory using a plain JavaScript object keyed by the company field on each row. No matter how many companies exist, this stays exactly one query against the database.

Second pitfall: using getRowCount just to check whether any records match. getRowCount doesn't avoid running the query — it runs the full query and then reports how many rows matched, so the database still does the complete work of finding every match even when you only needed a yes or no answer. When that's all you need, set a limit of 1 and check next once instead, so the database can stop at the very first match.

Third, setLimit matters whenever you only need a sample — say the 10 most recent incidents for a dashboard — instead of fetching every matching row and discarding the rest. And fourth, looping a full GlideRecord just to count or sum pulls every row's complete data for nothing. GlideAggregate is a separate, real ServiceNow API built specifically for COUNT, SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, and MAX — it never retrieves full row data at all, making it far more efficient for exactly this job.

N+1 loops, getRowCount misuse, missing setLimit, and looping instead of GlideAggregate — four real pitfalls, four real fixes. Next up, the lab: putting everything from this chapter together in one real, efficient Script Include method.
